articles.title: Meta’s new AI agent wants to make managing money easier
articles.description: Meta launched Muse, its new AI agent, earlier this month — and it's already claiming to help some consumers save money. At the 2026 Meta Connect conference, Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang spoke about Muse's ability to shop for products online, manage travel plans, save money on insurance costs, negotiate utility bills, and more. Now, he's challenging people to use Muse to save them $1,000 in what he's dubbed the #MuseMoneyChallenge on X. With the agent's help, users can do everything from create a budget to cancel unused subscriptions. Here's a closer look at Muse's personal finance capabilities, and some risks to weigh before handing over your financial information. Read more: Meta's Zuckerberg says Muse AI agent will take small fee from transactions What is Muse? Muse is Meta's personal AI agent. The company describes it as "an agent that takes on more of the work so people can focus on what matters to them." Plenty of other AI agents exist today with features that allow users to help with tasks — whether that's setting up a work meeting on a shared calendar, writing code, or planning a summer vacation. Instead of just chatting with users and responding to prompts, these agents can make decisions based on information already discussed and take actions on the user's behalf, generally based on parameters they've set. Many have also begun integrating personal finance tools for users. OpenAI's ChatGPT has a "personal finance experience" that lets you connect your financial information to get personalized recommendations and more. Robinhood has an agentic credit card feature that lets cardholders link their third-party AI agents to make automatic (preapproved) purchases. Read more: ChatGPT can now see your bank account. Is it worth the risk? Unlike some other AI agents, Muse is targeting everyday users, claiming to be the first personal AI agent "built for everyone" with "no learning curve." According to Meta ( META ), Muse can take on tasks that those already using agentic AI are familiar with, including sending emails, booking travel, and making restaurant reservations. It can also help users accomplish goals: "Once a person shares a goal with Muse, it helps them develop a personalized plan and coordinate their time and resources, then advances the work on its own. It can open a browser, fill out forms, and negotiate on their behalf." Meta is also positioning Muse specifically as a personal finance tool. Read more: Meta's Muse is an impressively capable AI agent, despite some hiccups How Meta's Muse could help with your finances Here are a few of the ways Muse can assist with personal finances: Track spending and saving When you connect your bank account to Muse, it can track your spending and help you set a budget. By reviewing your frequent purchases, it can recommend where to cut back and save more. You can also set up regular check-ins on spending and savings goals and have the agent make adjustments over time. Read more: Best high-yield savings accounts Audit subscriptions Muse can use your linked accounts to find all of the subscriptions you're currently paying for and help you decide what's worth keeping. Beyond the one-time audit, it can also keep monitoring your paid subscriptions so they don't pile up. The agent can even track unexpected expenses charged to your accounts, which can be useful if you forget to cancel a free trial before it turns into a paid subscription. Negotiate bills With access to financial accounts, Muse can analyze your bills and expenses to find any duplicate charges or errors and then resolve them for you. If there's a provider charging less for a service you already pay for, it can let you know. Muse can also negotiate lower bills for you. In some cases, it may be able to call your service providers and negotiate bill prices itself. Other times, it can start the process and connect you to the call to speak with a representative. Find money you're owed Muse can search online databases for unclaimed property , finding any money you're owed across different states you've lived in. It can file the claims for you and start the process of receiving the money — whether from old bank accounts, employers, overpaid utility bills, and more. Find deals Before you buy an item, Muse can search online for the best prices and recommend similar items at lower price points. It can also keep track of an item you've already purchased to see when prices drop. If the discount falls within your credit card's purchase protection policy, it can help you navigate the claim. If you choose, it can even make purchases for you. Muse is set up to ask for approval before it authorizes any spending. For websites where your payment method is already on file, it'll give you the purchase details and ask for approval before purchasing. If you don't already have a stored payment, Muse can use your stored payment (using single-use card information, but not sharing your real card numbers with the merchant) to make the purchase, again with your approval. Read more: Americans are using AI for financial advice more than you think Muse security and privacy risks For a lot of users, privacy is a major concern when it comes to using an AI agent — including Muse — for personal finance help. Experts we've spoken to are also skeptical about linking sensitive financial information to third-party services. "Right now, the technology is too new," Eva Velasquez, CEO of the Identity Theft Resource Center, recently told Yahoo Finance. "The data sharing implications are still unknown … It's just not something we're going to recommend." According to Meta, Muse has several built-in security protections. That includes securely storing passwords and payment methods (even from the agent itself), requiring approval for certain actions, keeping a trail of past and future actions, and more. Still, privacy isn't guaranteed. Meta itself admits Muse "isn't immune to attack" and "will sometimes make mistakes." If you're not willing to share your banking and credit card information yet, you can still make use of Muse for your personal finances. The process will just require more manual work on your end. Instead of allowing complete access to your credit card account, for example, you can upload a copy of your most recent statement, or several past statements, and omit information you want to keep private. The agent can use that select information to help you find recurring expenses, identify unnecessary spending, and create a budget. Read more: I asked ChatGPT for financial advice. Here's what happened. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Personal Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/personal-finance/banking/article/metas-muse-says-it-can-manage-your-money-should-you-let-it-141040045.html

articles.title: Stay motivated and healthy this school year
articles.description: With courseload ramping up, academic and personal stress has settled into most people's lives. Here are my best tips for staying disciplined, motivated, organized and, most importantly, happy and healthy this fall. 1) 3-2-1 method I often find that the transition phase between tasks is the hardest to overcome. If I'm in my bed and scrolling on my phone, the task of getting up and locking in seems daunting. To combat this, I use the 3-2-1 method: in my head, I'll count down from 3 and get up when I reach 1. This gives my mind something to do and distracts me while I get ready to start my task. I notice that after I begin, the work seems less stressful and I can truly concentrate. 2) Notes app I don't know if it's just me, but I hate using planners. The task of having to lug around a book with me at all times is hard for me to stick to. Instead, I utilize the Notes app on my phone that I sync with my computer. Being able to jot everything down at a moment's notice and organize when I get home is more convenient and effective. 3) Take breaks When you're on hour two or three of studying, your mind can lose focus easily. I find that taking a break is vastly beneficial. Different ways to take breaks: - Pomodoro method: 25 minutes of working followed by a five minute break, and repeat. You can find custom timers online, especially on Youtube, that can help set the aesthetic appeal of your study session (rain ambience is my favorite). - Switching between tasks: If you have more than one type of work to do, it's best to take breaks from one type of work to do another type of work. It gives different parts of your brain time to rest. For example, yesterday I had terms to memorize for psychology and a long article to read for my film class. I divided my time equally between the two, spending 25 minutes on one and then 25 minutes on another. I felt more refreshed and productive, and I was able to focus for longer. - Go for a walk: The most underrated form of taking a break. Sitting for long periods of time can slow your circulation and make you tired. Get your blood flowing on a walk, and you'll feel refreshed and ready to approach your work again with a fresh perspective. 4) Don't overload There are so many cool organizations here, and I would love if I could join them all. At the Student Involvement Fair, I definitely felt some serious decision fatigue. However, overloading yourself with work can be detrimental, and you'll often find that putting your energy into two or three things you're super passionate about is better than joining as many clubs as possible and doing half-hearted work. 5) Optimal sleep Contrary to popular belief, not all hours of the night are worth the same. Research from the Cleveland Health Clinic suggests that the best hours to be asleep are from 10pm to 2am, as that is when your body's natural circadian rhythm maximizes deep sleep and melatonin production. When given a choice, it's always better to prioritize sleep in this timeframe, even if that means having to wake up at an earlier time the next day to get work done. 6) Mindset is everything While hard work is valuable, nothing is more important than your physical and mental health. Working too hard can cause a multitude of issues, and no one gets an award for suffering. Instead of overloading yourself, constructing a schedule that maximizes your own personal health and happiness is the most important of all. Make sure to do the things you like, whether that be having fun with friends or setting aside time to do your favorite hobbies. With good time management, you can thrive. On campus, there are a multitude of resources to help if you are struggling. Go to this link to seek professional support if you are feeling down. It is never embarrassing to ask for help! Stay safe, Blue Jays, and have a good semester!

articles.title: Senate body orders probe into ‘overcharging’ by telco
articles.description: ISLAMABAD: The Senate Standing Committee on Information Technology and Telecommunication has constituted a subcommittee to investigate allegations that a leading telecom firm had charged customers Rs5.83 billion in excess of tariffs approved by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA). The subcommittee, headed by Senator Dr Afnanullah Khan, will examine the alleged overcharging by Jazz and the regulatory action taken by the PTA in the matter. The decision was taken following a heated debate between PTA officials and representatives of the Auditor General of Pakistan (AGP). Committee Chairperson Senator Palwasha Khan intervened to pacify the situation when the PTA chairman threatened to resign if any allegation of corruption was levelled against him. Meanwhile, a Jazz spokesperson said the matter concerned two government entities and that Jazz would present its point of view if called before any relevant forum. The matter relates to the audit of the PTA for 2024. The audit objection stated that the telecom regulator had allowed a 15 per cent tariff increase for Jazz against a permissible limit of 3pc. The audit also suggested seeking the opinion of the Competition Commission of Pakistan (CCP) on the tariff policy. PTA Chairman retired Maj Gen Hafeezur Rehman questioned the proposal, saying that if tariffs were to be decided by the CCP, the PTA should not be held responsible for ensuring quality of service. “Let them take the whole responsibility,” he said. He maintained that the regulator had acted with complete transparency in allowing the 15pc tariff increase for Jazz and offered to have the matter subjected to a forensic audit. The PTA chairman categorically stated that he would resign if even one rupee of overcharging by the telecom operator was established in violation of the authority’s approved tariffs. He explained that the PTA examined mobile packages before their launch and monitored compliance with the approved tariff structure. However, audit officials had raised certain queries regarding the matter. Senator Palwasha Khan subsequently decided to constitute the subcommittee. It will examine the relevant tariff approvals, packages and billing details to determine whether customers were charged amounts beyond the rates approved by the regulator. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

articles.title: Russia Crackdown on Bypassing Online Censorship
articles.description: Click to expand Image A person checks their phone in the Red Square in Moscow, Russia, March 31, 2026. © 2026 Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo (Berlin, September 24, 2026) – Russian authorities are doubling down on their efforts to quash freedom of expression, including access to information, by increasingly suppressing tools to circumvent draconian censorship laws, Human Rights Watch said today. Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) services face intensifying blocking and takedowns from app stores. “The Russian government’s escalating attacks on censorship circumvention services is part of its broader assault on access to information, privacy, and freedom of expression,” said Hugh Williamson, Europe and Central Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “These repressive tactics affect millions of people in Russia seeking to connect to the internet without state censorship.” On August 4, 2026, Exploit media outlet reported that 20 Virtual Private Network (VPN) providers in Russia had faced service disruptions caused by the blockings carried out by the Russian authorities. A representative of one of the affected VPN services told Human Rights Watch that the recent waves of blocking targeted VPN services’ infrastructure, namely, large blocks of IP addresses they use, including entire subnets of IP addresses allocated to them by their hosting service providers. Restoring VPN services following such bulk blocking can take more time and be more costly in comparison to previous more granular state blocking, the representative said. In June, the authorities carried out a coordinated attack targeting Amnezia VPN, one of the most popular VPN services in Russia. One of Amnezia’s developers said that the authorities blocked its IP addresses in bulk, targeted employees with phishing emails in an attempt to obtain sensitive data, and used distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks, which overwhelmed the service and disrupted its work. It took Amnezia one and a half months to fully restore its services. The new tactics in state crackdown on VPNs have created significant technical, financial, and operational challenges and damaged their reputation as reliable services, Human Rights Watch said. In April, the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media instructed more than 20 of the largest internet companies, which together provide digital services to the vast majority of Russians, to gather information on their clients’ VPN use and deny access to services when detecting VPN connections. According to a study published by RKS Global, a group of experts working on internet freedom, at least 30 of the largest Russian apps gathered this information. An expert at RKS Global told Human Rights Watch that the information included IP addresses used by the VPN services and was used in the recent attack on VPNs’ infrastructure. Over the past decade, VPNs have become a lifeline for accessing millions of censored websites in Russia, including to access independent media, foreign social media and messaging platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, and WhatsApp. Since spring 2025, the authorities have increasingly carried out “whitelists” shutdowns, blocking access to all but state approved websites. The 2017 law on VPN services prohibited them from providing access to state-blocked websites. By February 2026, the authorities had blocked at least 469 VPNs under this law. In 2025, the authorities banned advertising VPNs, introduced fines for “intentionally” searching for “extremist” content on the internet, including via VPNs, and classified the use of VPNs as an aggravating circumstance with regard to certain crimes. Nevertheless, the number of VPN downloads consistently grows, and about 40 percent of Russia’s population—57 million people—are estimated to use VPN. In addition to direct blocking, Russian authorities increasingly pressure foreign technology companies to take down VPN apps from their app stores, Human Rights Watch said. In its transparency report, Apple said that in 2025 it removed 468 “utility” applications, which includes VPNs, from its App Store. Overall, 1,213 applications were removed in response to Russian government requests, nearly 60 percent of all such removals globally. In March 2026, Apple removed several popular VPNs—Streisand, V2Box, v2RayTun, Happ, and Proxy Utility—from its App Store. v2RayTun shared Apple’s removal notification, which cited a demand from Roskomnadzor, the state media and communications watchdog, on the grounds that the application “included content that is illegal in Russia.” The notice referred to part 7 of article 15.1 of Russia’s Law on Information, which the Russian authorities widely use to restrict privacy, freedom of expression, and access to information online. In March 2026, the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media ordered the four largest mobile service providers in the country to stop allowing payments to Apple account holders using mobile phone billing, a popular method for paying for VPNs. In July, Human Rights Watch sent a letter to Apple, inquiring about company policy on VPN takedowns in Russia, as well as the exact number of VPNs taken down by Apple on the authorities’ demand. Apple responded that “[Apple is] required to follow the law everywhere we operate, even where we may disagree with a country’s laws. In Russia, failure to comply with lawful orders could result in Apple no longer being able to operate the App Store or distribute content in the country, and we believe that would not be in the best interests of our users, because the App Store remains an important platform for Russian users to access information.” Russian authorities also repeatedly demanded that Google take down hundreds of VPN apps from its Play Store. In February, a Russian court fined Google 22.8 million rubles (around USD 300,000) for failure to remove VPN apps as authorities ordered. In July, both Apple and Google faced apparent blocking in Russia. VPNs that do not collect their clients’ logs, or digital footprint, and do not transfer data to state authorities can ensure privacy of internet communications for their users, including against the advanced state surveillance system in Russia, Human Rights Watch said. By escalating their blocking of VPNs, the authorities push users to repeatedly change VPN service providers, with privacy and security risks, such as choosing a VPN service that stores data without their consent, or shares data with Russian authorities. Multiple United Nations human rights institutions condemn restrictions on anonymity, including the blocking of VPNs, that are essential for safeguarding rights online, as violating the right to privacy, freedom of expression, access to information, the right to peaceful assembly, and other rights and freedoms. The 2015 UN Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of the right to freedom of opinion and expression said in a report that anonymity and encryption are key for freedom of opinion and expression, and that blanket prohibitions fail necessity and proportionality criteria. Foreign technology companies should resist Russian government pressure to take down VPNs from their app stores. Governments, intergovernmental institutions, groups, and foundations concerned with promoting human rights including freedom of expression, access to information, and other internet freedoms should continue developing and supporting the tools that maximize privacy, ensure anonymity, and enable internet users in Russia to circumvent draconian internet censorship. “With the government escalating attacks on digital rights, it is crucial for groups working to ensure uncensored access to the internet in Russia receive financial, institutional, and other essential support,” Williamson said.
